# Tool-Connected Design Environments {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."*
>
> —  John Culkin, *Saturday Review* (1967) [@Culkin1967Schoolman]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** John Culkin, an American media scholar writing to explain
Marshall McLuhan's ideas, used the line to describe how tools reshape human
practice. An architecture tool likewise shapes what a method can change and
what an architect can observe. Those limits must be explicit when the method
acts through the tool.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What must surround real architecture tools so an artificial intelligence
(AI)-assisted method can use them safely, reproducibly, and within declared
limits?
:::

A tool command is not an environment. An architect can launch a simulator,
compiler, formal engine, or physical-design flow and still be unable to say
which candidate ran, which state the tool inherited, what an unfamiliar
warning meant, or whether a retry repeated the same work. AI-assisted methods
make this gap harder to ignore because they can issue requests faster than a
person can inspect the state around every invocation.

Consider a cache-capacity comparison in which a quick static random-access
memory (SRAM) evaluation screens each candidate before the eligible designs
enter a small budget of cycle-level runs. The tools would need to return
physical estimates, matched workload results, warnings, failures, and realized
cost. A run that loses candidate identity or mismatches conditions could return
plausible values for the wrong comparison, while an unbounded retry could spend
more than the declared study budget.

The request is precise enough to select tools, but it is not executable yet.
Each represented candidate must become the exact configuration each tool
expects. Workload, software, libraries, process assumptions, and tool versions
must travel with it. Long jobs enter queues and may wait for licenses. A tool
may crash, time out, finish with a missing report, or exit successfully after
running the wrong top-level design. Returned files may arrive hours later and
out of order.

The environment handles those mechanics. It establishes that requested work
reached a named tool against a named state and records what the attempt
produced. It does not establish that the resulting number is a valid
measurement or that the candidate is good. This distinction separates a
well-formed run from a supported architecture claim. Interpreting the return
and judging the claim require additional checks beyond the environment.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Distinguish tools and simulators from their wrappers, harnesses, and enclosing environments.
- Pin environment state across hardware, software, and tools to guarantee reproducible execution.
- Design typed tool interfaces that precisely translate intent and return structured artifacts.
- Coordinate multi-tool asynchronous workflows within strict resource and permission boundaries.
- Separate execution failures from design-limit violations while preserving lineage.
:::

## Tools, Wrappers, Harnesses, and Environments

No single component carries a request from represented design state to an
identifiable tool return. Five terms separate the responsibilities along that
path.

- A *tool* transforms an artifact or analyzes a stated property under declared
  inputs and conditions. Compilers, SRAM models, simulators, formal engines,
  synthesis tools, and place-and-route flows are tools.
- A *simulator* is one kind of tool. It executes a model of hardware and
  software behavior and returns only the behavior that model exposes. It is not
  the complete environment.
- A *wrapper* surrounds one tool. It validates a request, translates the
  request into tool-specific inputs, invokes the tool, and parses the returned
  files.
- A *harness* coordinates the wrappers and records attempts, state, costs,
  failures, retries, resets, and produced artifacts.
- The *environment* is everything that connects the study to its tools. It
  defines the state a method may observe, the requests it may issue, the tools
  it may reach, and the returns it may receive.

One environment may contain wrappers for an SRAM model, a cycle-level
simulator, a cache model, and a power model. One harness keeps their outputs
tied to the same candidate and conditions.

The distinction is structural rather than cosmetic. A simulator remains a tool
even when it has a Python interface. A wrapper still serves one tool. A harness
can coordinate several wrappers, but it becomes part of an environment only
when the study can inspect relevant state, issue bounded requests, and receive
identifiable returns through it.

Each request must survive the full path from known starting state to
identifiable return. Setup establishes the design, software, workload, tool,
and resource state. Interfaces and wrappers define what may be requested and
translate it exactly. The runtime and harness schedule, isolate, budget,
cancel, retry, and record the work. The return includes execution status,
artifacts, parsed results, warnings, cost, and lineage. These jobs remain the
same whether a learned method, a conventional search, or an architect issues
the request.

A broader design workflow uses the environment but does not belong to it. The
workflow owns the ordering of design work, method decisions, interpretation of
returned results, and human review. The environment executes authorized
requests and exposes identifiable returns to that workflow.

A caller must be able to inspect the candidate, fixed state, supported tool
operations, resources, and prior attempts before submitting work. The
environment then accepts only declared requests and returns execution status,
raw artifacts, parsed fields, unclassified output, cost, and lineage. Request
checking, tool execution, parsing, and run recording remain separate
responsibilities throughout that path (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

![**A tool interface separates execution state from interpretation.** The
wrapper validates and translates the request, the tool executes the declared
operation, the parser interprets retained output, and the harness records both
the runtime outcome and parse status.](images/F6-environment-tool-interface){#fig-environment-tool-interface fig-alt="An architecture question and workload, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter a tool-connected environment as a typed request. A wrapper validates and translates the request before calling the tool. An invalid request goes directly to the harness record. The tool separately produces raw returned material and a runtime outcome that can be failed, partial, or complete. A parser turns retained raw material into structured fields, unclassified residual output, and a parse status. The harness records request and attempt identity, conditions, runtime outcome, artifacts, parse status, cost, and lineage."}

The represented question and state enter the interface as a typed request. The
wrapper either refuses an invalid request or translates it to the declared tool
path. A valid invocation produces raw returned material and a runtime outcome.
The parser keeps recognized fields, residual output, and its own interpretation
status, while the harness records those fields alongside the execution outcome,
identity, cost, and lineage. A parser failure therefore does not rewrite a
complete tool invocation as a tool failure, and a clean parse cannot turn a
partial tool return into a complete one.

Building this environment is difficult because an architecture tool inherits
state that the request never names and returns more material than the request
asked for.

## Architecture Tools Carry State and Return Partial Results

Architecture tools do not behave like interchangeable stateless services.
They operate on large, versioned artifacts; preserve hidden state in working
directories and databases; use incompatible formats and units; wait for shared
machines and licenses; and produce partial files after long failures. A single
candidate may require software construction, simulation,
register-transfer-level (RTL) models, formal checks, synthesis, and physical
implementation. No generic software sandbox supplies those architecture
meanings automatically.

OpenROAD exposes Tcl and Python command interfaces over a stateful design
database [@OpenROADDocs]. A wrapper for such a tool must establish or validate
the declared state before each invocation, use the tool's error mechanism to
return an explicit status, and serialize the recognized fields. It must also
retain the raw transcript and any unclassified output. A clean structured
record is useful, but it is not sufficient if an unfamiliar warning was
discarded while the record was built.

Real projects also inherit intellectual property (IP) blocks, software,
constraints, generated files, vendor models, and tool databases. The
environment need not reveal protected contents beyond the study's
authorization, but it must preserve the exact identity, version, permitted
use, and dependent state carried into each invocation. Otherwise a repeated
request can appear identical while running against a different design or
model.

An implementation flow illustrates the problem. OpenROAD provides
`read_liberty` for loading Liberty libraries and `read_lef` for loading Library
Exchange Format (LEF) technology and macro data [@OpenROADDocs]. One legacy
SRAM macro may also appear as a behavioral model in simulation, a Liberty timing
and power view during synthesis and timing analysis, and a LEF physical view
during placement and routing. Updating the behavioral model while retaining an
older Liberty or LEF view lets different tool stages evaluate different
versions of what the study treats as one macro. The environment must bind
compatible views to one identity or refuse the run.

Translation must be exact or refused. If the study asks for `l2.capacity=3MiB`,
the wrapper may serialize that value into an SRAM configuration file and a
simulator parameter. It may not silently round the value to the nearest
supported capacity, change associativity to make the configuration legal, or
substitute another simulator because it is idle. Each of those choices changes
the meaning of the request. A syntax-preserving repair may create a new request
artifact or execution attempt while retaining the candidate identity. The
wrapper refuses a repair that would change architecture meaning and returns the
validation failure to the candidate-producing caller. That caller, under the
enclosing lifecycle, may create a new candidate. Method selection reopens only
if the failure invalidates the chosen approach or its supported action space.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One cache request, several exact translations"}
The 3\ MiB candidate becomes one SRAM-model input under the declared process,
voltage, and temperature conditions and, if the predeclared routing condition
permits, one cycle-level simulator configuration linked to the declared cache
and power models, XR workload trace, and baseline software image. The wrapper
may change file syntax, paths, and command-line spelling. It may not change
cache policy, associativity, the network-on-chip (NoC), compiler, runtime,
workload, or another architecture field. An exact translation proceeds.
Anything else is refused and recorded.
:::

This narrow rule prevents a common failure. An automated repair can make a
tool call legal by changing the design that was supposed to be evaluated. The
tool then runs cleanly, but the returned result belongs to a different
candidate. Request validation should catch the mismatch before cluster time is
spent. Exact validation first requires an identifiable starting state.

## Setup, State, and Lineage

Every requested run begins from a known state. Source and generated artifacts,
workload inputs, tool and library versions, process design kit (PDK) views,
constraints, environment variables, host resources, and baseline artifacts
must be pinned or marked intentionally variable before the first tool starts.
The run specification fixes the relationship among that state, the represented
request, the tool path, and the returned artifacts. It says how the requested
work will run without changing the architecture comparison.

*Lineage* is the parent-child history that connects requests, transformations,
and artifacts. It lets another architect determine which inputs produced a
return and whether a later retry, software image, or hardware artifact belongs
to the same candidate.

Pinned state is necessary but still inadequate. A retry can repeat billable
work, a failed process can contaminate the next attempt, a reset can restore the
wrong baseline, and reused output can cross candidate or condition boundaries.
Failure, retry, reset, containment, and retention rules must therefore keep
runtime behavior from changing the request's meaning or realized cost. The
prospective cache-study run specification in @tbl-environment-contract gathers
these responsibilities into one concrete example.

Immutable inputs are the versioned source, workload snapshot, constraints,
libraries, PDK views, tool images, and baseline artifacts from which a run
starts. Mutable work state is the run directory, generated files, tool
database, checkpoint, scheduler state, and other state the requested action may
change. The harness never patches the immutable inputs in place. It creates a
new working state linked to them and records every permitted mutation.

Reset means restoring a declared starting state, not merely calling a function
named `reset`. A clean reset regenerates the working directory and tool state
from pinned inputs. A checkpoint reset starts from an identified intermediate
database whose parent inputs and validity conditions still match. Setup checks
must confirm the expected top level, clocks, constraints, libraries, workload,
tool version, and artifact set before scarce execution begins.

Architecture tools rarely consume the representation in which the study was
formulated. An SRAM model reads an organization and technology configuration.
A cycle-level simulator reads a platform description, workload image, and
microarchitecture and platform parameters. A power model may consume activity
and event counts from another tool. The environment lowers one candidate into
these forms while retaining the parent relationship.

A complete transformation record tracks these identities and outcomes.

- the parent candidate and request;
- the transformation and tool version;
- input identifiers and content hashes where useful;
- fixed conditions inherited from the study;
- the output artifact and its hash;
- whether the transformation preserved architecture meaning; and
- the next authorized consumer.

Serialization that changes only syntax keeps the candidate identity. This
distinction matters when a wrapper repairs a malformed file. Adding a missing
quote around `3MiB` may preserve meaning. Reducing the cache to `2MiB` so the
parser accepts it does not.

Content hashes make exact artifacts distinguishable. They do not prove that
two artifacts are functionally equivalent or represent the same architecture.
Bazel provides one example of a build system that uses declared dependencies
and cached actions [@Bazel2026Dependencies; @Bazel2026RemoteCaching].
Even with that discipline, undeclared tool state can still
defeat reproducibility, so the harness records the execution conditions as well
as the hash.

Seeds are only one variation control. The setup should also pin thread counts,
scheduler placement, parallel reduction order, host libraries, and the timing
of concurrent jobs where the tool permits. A tool may require additional
controls when its documentation identifies a nondeterministic algorithm or
heuristic. Where a factor cannot be fixed, the execution record states what
varied and retains enough repeated attempts to characterize repeatability
later. Declared variation can be studied; unrecorded variation is an unknown
dependency.

A larger hardware and software change makes the lineage problem visible
(@fig-artifact-lineage). The same root intent may produce several software
binaries and RTL artifacts.

![**Every evaluated artifact needs an identifiable parent.** Software and
hardware artifacts derived from one proposal retain their transformation
history, and a changed input creates a new evaluation
identity.](images/F5-artifact-lineage){#fig-artifact-lineage fig-alt="One Lighthouse intent branches into a software variant and a hardware variant. The software compiles into an identified binary, and the hardware elaborates into an identified RTL artifact. One evaluation instance binds both artifacts to the tool and version, workload, and operating conditions. Hashes and evaluation keys distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

In the displayed branch, the Lighthouse intent produces one software variant
and one hardware variant. The software variant compiles into an identified
binary, while the hardware variant elaborates into an identified RTL artifact.
The selected pair becomes one evaluation instance. Replacing either child
creates a different pair even when the root intent does not change. The
artifact hashes distinguish the exact files and their transformation path. The
evaluation key additionally binds the pair to the tool and version, workload,
and operating conditions. These identities still do not establish functional
equivalence or reproducibility when relevant state remains undeclared.

Conditions can invalidate an identity match just as quickly as stale
artifacts. An SRAM-model return carries circuit and technology assumptions
under its declared process, voltage, and temperature conditions. An
implementation return carries its corner, mode, libraries, constraints, and
flags. Cycle-level simulation, cache-model, and power-model returns carry
workload, software, warm-up, region, seed, checkpoint, and model configuration.
The environment retains the conditions that apply to each tool and marks
nonapplicable fields without judging whether the conditions are sufficient. A
timing-slack return of $-12\,\mathrm{ps}$ at a slow process corner is not
interchangeable with the same numeric return at a typical corner. The number
travels with the condition that gives it meaning.

The host environment can also change a result. Mytkowicz and colleagues showed
that link order and UNIX environment size can perturb measured performance by
more than many reported optimizations [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. An optimizer
with many attempts can exploit such effects. Pinning and recording the binary,
host, environment, and flags prevents an accidental host difference from
masquerading as a candidate difference.

Pinned state establishes what a run starts from. A wrapper must now expose the
change a method is allowed to request without erasing the meaning of the
tool-specific return.

## Interfaces and Tool Wrappers

A wrapper turns the known starting state into one narrow tool interface. Its
request schema names every parameter, type, unit, required input, default, and
legal combination. Its return schema names every structured field, unit,
status, warning class, and raw artifact. A capacity field that means bytes must
not accept an unqualified `3`; a timing result must not omit whether its unit
is cycles, nanoseconds, or simulator ticks.

A usable interface distinguishes state from what the caller can observe.
*State* is the relevant condition of the design, software, tools, runtime,
resources, and outstanding work. An *observation* is the authorized portion of
that state, or a returned result, exposed to the caller. An *action* is a
permitted typed request with identity and preconditions. A *transition* records
what changed when an action was accepted, completed, failed, canceled, or
reset. A tool *return* combines the raw and structured output of one attempt
with its execution status. @sec-feedback-verification-trust determines whether
any returned field can support a measurement, update, or stopping decision.

The interface must also state which project state the caller may read and
which fields it may change. A cache-sizing wrapper can expose capacity while
keeping associativity, policy, interconnect, compiler, runtime, and workload
read-only. The wrapper refuses a request outside that action set. It does not
silently project the request to the nearest supported design.

Shared fields remove accidental interface differences without hiding tool
meaning. The same request identity, allowed actions, job status, errors, cost,
cancellation, retry, and lineage fields let several methods use one tool path
under common action and budget rules. They also let one method move among
compatible tool paths without reimplementing scheduling and failure handling.
The resulting request and execution records are comparable across methods, but
the measurements, candidate quality, and conclusions are not. A wrapper or
tool path is replaceable only when its declared capabilities, properties,
conditions, schemas, and semantics are compatible. Each wrapper must still
expose its supported operations, stages, properties, fidelities, units,
assumptions, defaults, and warnings.

Capability and schema discovery make that division inspectable. Each request
and return records the wrapper, request-schema, return-schema, parser, and tool
versions. A caller can inspect supported actions and fields before submitting
work. An unsupported request is refused rather than silently dropping a field,
changing a default, or substituting another fidelity. A retained request is
never reinterpreted under a newer schema. An explicit migration creates a new
request artifact linked to the original.

Errors are part of the interface. Validation errors, tool diagnostics, missing
outputs, parse failures, and unclassified warnings remain distinct and retain
their original text. A typed result makes routine fields easier to consume, but
the wrapper must not discard output that its current schema does not recognize.
Keeping raw output, parsed fields, execution outcomes, and run identity on
separate paths prevents one component from silently assigning meaning to
another component's result (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

The environment need not return a scalar reward. A method may later derive an
objective or reward from returned values, but the derived value remains
separate from the raw observations and cannot replace them. A shared interface
therefore standardizes how work is requested and returned while leaving
architecture objectives and interpretation outside the wrapper.

Structured hardware representations can reduce ambiguity when they match the
artifact. Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) documents hardware dialects
and compiler passes that operate on structured intermediate representations
rather than requiring every change to be a textual source edit [@CIRCT]. That
is a useful interface technique, not the definition of an environment. Nor
does a shared CIRCT operation, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schema, or
simulator request make two tools equal in fidelity. The tool model, setup, and
returned property still determine what each observation contains.

Before a wrapper becomes part of a study, the project should test its
translation and control path with known fixtures. Each fixture pairs a typed
request with the expected command, translated inputs, retained artifacts, and
parsed return. Legal cases should match the values reported by tool
introspection or preserved in the translated input, while illegal requests
should be refused. These checks catch silent defaults, unit conversions, stale
working state, and parsers that accept output from the wrong run.

Failure injection exercises the mechanics that routine runs seldom reach. The
harness can force a timeout, kill a process, omit or truncate output, and leave
stale state, then check cancellation, retry, reset, and parsing behavior. The
project should rerun these tests when a wrapper, parser, schema, library, or tool
version changes. For the requests, faults, states, and tool versions they
exercise, passing tests establishes only that translation, control, state, and
parsing behave as declared. Untested combinations remain unknown.

Cloud systems provide a useful precedent. FATE and DESTINI inject faults to
exercise recovery paths and check whether the resulting behavior matches a
declared recovery policy [@GunawiEtAl2011FATEDestini]. An EDA wrapper can adopt
that testing idea, but the cloud result does not establish that the wrapper
preserves architecture meaning, covers tool-specific failure modes, or makes a
recovery retry safe. Those claims still require fixtures and faults tied to the
actual tool path.

Once a request crosses the tested interface, the runtime must keep its identity
intact while the work waits, runs, fails, or returns.

## Coordinating and Containing Tool Runs

Architecture work rarely fits one blocking function call. Cycle simulations
may run for hours. Physical-design jobs may wait in queues, hold scarce
licenses, produce intermediate databases, or fail after substantial work.
Tool state persists in working directories, caches, checkpoints, license
servers, random seeds, and generated artifacts, while outputs may return
asynchronously or out of order. One tool path may also depend on an artifact
produced by another.

A familiar reinforcement-learning environment presents a synchronous
`step()` interface that returns an observation, reward, termination flags, and
auxiliary information [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium]. Architecture execution cannot
usually be reduced to that exchange. The runtime must preserve the queueing,
dependency, persistent state, and ordering behavior above and the typed tool
return. A method can derive a reward afterward when one is needed.

The harness reaches a scheduler or execution backend through a *scheduler
adapter*. The adapter maps stable harness operations such as submit, inspect
status, and cancel onto one backend. It does not replace a tool wrapper, which
still owns tool-specific validation, translation, invocation, and parsing.

At minimum, a caller must be able to inspect capabilities and state, submit a
typed request, receive an attempt identifier, inspect or cancel that attempt,
and receive its raw and parsed return, status, warnings, cost, and lineage.
One request can produce no backend job, one job, or several jobs or execution
segments. These cases still belong to one attempt, and that attempt retains
separate fields for how work was scheduled, why it ended, what artifacts exist,
what the parser recognized, whether cancellation completed, and which prior
attempt authorized a retry. The object relationships remain visible in
@fig-runtime-object-state.

![**One attempt can contain zero, one, or several backend executions.** The
attempt record keeps backend work attached to the authorized request while
preserving returned artifacts, realized cost, and independent status fields.](images/F6c-runtime-object-state){#fig-runtime-object-state fig-alt="An authorized request creates one attempt. The attempt may be refused before a backend job exists, may create one job, or may create several jobs or execution segments. All paths feed one attempt record. The attempt record points separately to returned artifacts and realized cost. Scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, cancellation confirmation, and retry parent remain independent fields."}

The figure separates object identity from state classification. A request that
fails admission still leaves an attempt record even though no scheduler job
exists. A multi-stage physical-design invocation may create several backend
segments without becoming several candidates. Returned artifacts and realized
cost remain attached to the attempt, including work that failed, was canceled,
or was retried. Keeping the six status fields independent prevents a terminal
process state from implying complete artifacts, a successful parse, or
confirmed cancellation.

### Attempts, Jobs, and Dependencies

One request specifies an allowed action for a candidate under declared
conditions. Each authorized try is an attempt. Every job and segment retains
the attempt identifier. A planned repeat is an intentional new attempt required
by the study, while a recovery retry is a new attempt authorized because prior
execution failed or
returned incompletely. The Recovery section later in the chapter develops the
detailed retry policy.

The harness attaches every job or segment to its attempt at submission, before
a late result can arrive. Dependencies remain explicit. A compiler build may
wait for a source artifact, RTL simulation may wait for elaboration, and
physical implementation may wait for a mapped netlist. Independent jobs may
run concurrently, but concurrency does not relax their identity or resource
limits.

The scheduler may accept work before the harness records its job identifier.
The harness therefore tags submitted work with the attempt identifier and
reconciles its record with the scheduler before resubmitting. An *idempotency
key* is a request identifier whose durable backend handling prevents a repeated
submission from launching the same work twice. Here, `submission_token` serves
that role. The backend records the key with the first admission result, and a
later submission with the same key identifies the existing attempt or job. The
harness retains the key through the retry window, reconciles it after a crash,
and rejects its reuse for a different request [@Featonby2021IdempotentAPIs].

A backend status of `running` does not establish useful progress. Where the
tool or backend exposes them, the harness retains advisory fields such as the
last heartbeat or output time, current tool stage or checkpoint, and resources
or licenses still held. These fields can support escalation or cancellation,
but they do not prove architecture progress or make a returned result valid.

### Authority, Budgets, and Cancellation

Authorization follows the established security principle of least privilege
[@SaltzerSchroeder1975ProtectionInformation]. A wrapper receives only the
executables, filesystem paths, network destinations, credentials, secrets,
licensed features, and intellectual property needed for its declared action.
Generated scripts, constraints, RTL, and compiler inputs are untrusted until
validated and confined. Each attempt uses an isolated working area, resource
limits, and a process boundary.

The same confinement applies to the material supplied to a model as well as to
tool processes.
Projects use segregated workspaces, retrieval indexes, caches and checkpoints,
model context, logs, and credentials, with each resource scoped to its project,
permissions, confidentiality limits, and retention policy. The wrapper selects
an authorized context set for each request, permits only declared egress routes,
and refuses to send material not explicitly authorized to cross the destination
boundary.
It reuses caches or checkpoints across scopes only when their identities and
permissions match. These controls reduce accidental mixing and disclosure.
Source permission and generated-output provenance still require separate
review.

Budgets apply independently to model calls, tool submissions, elapsed time,
CPU and accelerator use, memory, storage, and license occupancy. Admission
checks reserve scarce resources before dispatch. An accepted request may still
be queued, canceled, or fail. A completed run may still be missing an
artifact. These states determine what the runtime records and which recovery
actions remain available.

Automated work shares queues, machines, storage, and licenses with engineers
and production flows. When those resources saturate, the environment applies
the site's in-flight limits, project quotas or priorities, reservations, and
backpressure to slow or refuse new work. It exposes pending work, accepted
work, and remaining authorization so a method does not resubmit merely because
a queued job is not yet visible.

Cancellation is not complete when a request to stop has been issued. The
harness requests termination of descendants, then confirms process termination
and license release. A process may stop after producing partial artifacts or
may complete before cancellation takes effect. Any late return remains attached
to its original attempt and stays out of live state until the current request
revision and budget policy admit it.

Every attempt has a finite deadline for confirming a terminal state. A timeout
states whether it bounds queue wait, run time, one tool stage, or an absolute
deadline. If scheduler and process states disagree or remain unknown past that
deadline, the harness retains an unconfirmed attempt, quarantines uncertain
outputs, and prevents late writers from changing live state. It also preserves
enough partial state to explain what happened. This confirmation step is what
turns a cancellation request or timeout into a controlled runtime outcome.

### Returned State and Realized Cost

The execution interface keeps the request identifiable through validation,
admission, scheduling, termination, artifact inspection, and parsing. In the
common case, one attempt produces one scheduler job, but the record keeps those
stages and their outcomes distinct.

The record must answer what was requested, what actually ran, how it ended, and
what it cost. The request and run specification define the authorized work.
Attempt, job, and segment identifiers show what reached a backend. The attempt
record joins those objects to the returned material and realized cost. Keeping
them separate prevents a retry from becoming a new candidate or a scheduler job
from becoming an architecture result.

`candidate_id` names the architecture candidate across tool paths.
`configuration_id` names that candidate's declared tool-specific configuration
record for the requested path, not the translated files. Those files receive
separate artifact identifiers and hashes after validation. Both identities are
retained because one candidate may require several tool-specific
configurations, while several attempts may execute the same candidate and
configuration.

Before submission, the harness retains the request, authorized attempt, and
translated inputs. An invalid translation, unmet setup dependency, exhausted
budget, or refused admission produces an attempt record with no scheduler job
rather than disappearing from the record. Once the backend accepts the work,
the harness links the job to the attempt while it is queued, running, and
terminal. A terminal process still requires artifact inspection and parsing.

After the process stops, the same attempt record retains the terminal cause,
expected-artifact check, parser status, raw and structured output, retry
eligibility, resource use, cost, and lineage. Keeping those fields separate
lets the runtime distinguish a tool crash from a missing report or an outdated
parser.

The harness records resources separately instead of collapsing them into one
cost value. It keeps tool and candidate identity with submission, queue, start,
completion, and elapsed times; central processing unit (CPU) and accelerator
use; peak memory and storage; license occupancy; model and tool calls; retries
and cancellations; and linked setup, diagnosis, review, and repair work.

For scheduler-managed resources, the record distinguishes reserved, consumed,
and billable amounts when available, gives their units, and names the
scheduler, license server, or billing system that supplied each value. Fields
that the environment cannot observe remain explicitly unreported. Human work
may attach to a group of attempts when one setup or diagnosis supports several
invocations.

The decisive distinction is between one identified candidate-configuration
pair and the attempts used to execute it. A retry of the same pair increases
realized cost but does not create another candidate, tool-specific
configuration, or independent observation. The recorded setup and cost must
travel with any returned value that later becomes data. A later study can then
compare time, compute, storage, and license use without treating a cycle
simulation, a physical-design run, and a model call as equivalent samples.

Before choosing a retry, reset, checkpoint, or cached artifact, the harness must
first determine what the attempt returned. The runtime establishes what ran,
what returned, and what the work cost. It does not establish that a returned
value is valid or that the candidate should advance.

## Failure Returns and Tool-Output Parsing

Tool paths fail in several ways, and one `FAILED` value cannot represent them.
Terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and retry eligibility
remain separate fields. The rows below show common combinations rather than
one exclusive status value. They determine what the harness repairs and what
it hands forward, so they describe execution rather than architecture judgment
(@tbl-failure-taxonomy).

Formal tools make that separation especially important. Model-checking
variants may report different outcomes and attach different assumptions,
bounds, or artifacts [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. The environment preserves the
exact terminology reported by each formal method and tool, including theorem
provers and equivalence tools, rather than translating every completed formal
run into one generic status.

| **Execution outcome** | **How it appears** | **What the harness preserves** | **Runtime response** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Invalid request** | An illegal value, missing identity, or meaning-changing translation is found before invocation. | Request, validation rule, and refusal reason. | Repair syntax only when meaning is preserved; otherwise refuse the request and return it to the candidate-producing caller. Reopen method selection only if the failure invalidates the chosen approach or its supported action space. |
| **Setup or dependency failure** | The top level, clock, library, constraint, checkpoint, or generated input is missing or stale. | Setup check, diagnostics, partial artifacts, and realized cost. | Restore or regenerate the declared state. The candidate remains unevaluated. |
| **Infrastructure failure** | A license, host, scheduler, or storage service is unavailable. | Attempt, failure source, partial artifacts, cost, and retry eligibility. | Retry only under the declared policy. The candidate remains unevaluated. |
| **Tool failure** | The tool crashes, reports an internal error, or exhausts a local resource. | Tool status, diagnostics, partial artifacts, conditions, cost, and retry history. | Retry, reset, resume a valid checkpoint, or stop. Repetition does not prove physical infeasibility. |
| **Incomplete return** | A stage or expected report is missing, stale, or only partly written. | Completed stages, expected-artifact check, produced files, raw output, and parse status. | Preserve the partial return and repair or rerun before treating it as complete. |
| **Parser failure** | A retained artifact does not match the declared schema or contains unclassified output. | Parser version, raw artifact, diagnostics, recognized fields, and residual output. | Repair the parser and reparse the retained artifact when safe. |
| **Formal-tool return** | The declared method and tool report their exact outcome, which may include a proof, counterexample, bounded result, `unknown`, or resource limit. | Method, property or relation, model, assumptions, bound where applicable, tool, exact outcome, artifact, and cost. | Hand the method-specific result forward without turning it into a general correctness verdict. |
| **Reported design-limit violation** | A completed run reports a timing, power, congestion, design-rule, or functional violation. | Typed violation, units, candidate, conditions, warnings, raw artifact, and cost. | Record a complete return without rejecting or penalizing the candidate. |
| **Complete tool return** | Expected artifacts exist and parse, including reports that contain violations. | Typed fields, units, conditions, warnings, raw artifacts, cost, and lineage. | Retain the return for measurement qualification without deciding what it establishes. |

: **Execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.**
Invalid requests, failed paths, partial returns, parser failures, and complete
returns stay separate so the next repair targets the right problem.
{#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[18,25,31,26]"}

The execution condition determines both the retained record and the next
action. Invalid requests, setup failures, and infrastructure failures leave the
candidate unevaluated. Tool, artifact, and parser failures require different
owners to repair them. A formal-tool return and a reported design-limit
violation are completed returns, not process failures, but neither supplies a
broad design verdict. Every completed result goes forward with its scope
intact.

A clean exit becomes a complete tool return only after the expected-artifact
check and parser succeed. Consider a synthesis script that selects no valid
top-level module and omits the primary clock. The process may still exit zero
and produce empty reports. The harness records a completed process together
with missing artifacts and failed setup checks rather than substituting zeros
for area, power, and timing.

Physical-design stages show why a complete return may still contain a reported
limit violation. Logic synthesis returns a mapped netlist, constraints,
warnings, and early area and timing estimates, but no placed or routed
interconnect. Floorplanning and placement add locations, utilization,
congestion estimates, and a tool database, while clocking, routing, and power
analysis add stage-specific timing, design-rule, congestion, and power results
[@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD; @OpenROADDocs].
The harness records which stage produced each artifact so an early estimate
cannot masquerade as a later report.

Signoff returns remain tied to the tool, libraries, corner, mode, constraints,
warnings, and waivers that produced them. They do not cover properties or
conditions that were never run. Even a complete signoff return supplies neither
architecture interpretation nor authorization to proceed.

Raw logs remain part of the return. A commercial EDA tool or a detailed
simulator may emit long logs. A language model can miss relevant text in a long
context [@Liu2024LostInTheMiddle]. Discarding everything outside a fixed parser
is also unsafe. The wrapper should return structured fields for recognized
metrics and failures, an explicitly marked residual of unclassified warnings
and errors, and both a retrievable artifact identifier and integrity hash for
the complete raw log.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The parser recognizes only yesterday's warnings"}
**The trap.** A parser keeps only known warning classes and drops every line it
cannot classify.

**The mechanism.** A new warning about a downgraded timing constraint or
changed clock definition appears after a tool upgrade. The parser produces a
clean structured record because it was never taught the new class.

**The lesson.** Preserve unclassified warning and error lines with the raw log.
A compact return should reduce reading cost without granting the parser
permission to decide that unfamiliar output is irrelevant.
:::

The same rule applies to partial returns. A placement density map produced
before a router crash may help later diagnosis, but it remains a partial
artifact. The environment records what stage produced it and what never ran.
Later measurement qualification determines whether that artifact bears on any
claim.

Once these outcomes are classified, the harness can choose an allowed repair,
retry, reset, checkpoint resume, cache reuse, or refusal without treating a
complete return as failed work.

## Recovery, Reuse, and Isolation

A recovery retry is a new attempt linked to the failed or incomplete attempt,
not a continuation that erases what happened. It differs from a planned repeat,
which the study requests independently of failure. The record states which
inputs were reused, which state was reset, which checkpoint was resumed, and
why another attempt was authorized. A scheduler pause that continues the same
submitted job retains its identity; an authorized restart from a checkpoint or
a clean reset creates a linked attempt. Repeated failure under controlled
conditions may expose a reproducible tool problem, but it does not prove
physical infeasibility.

Recovery follows the failure class. Invalid requests are repaired before a
tool runs; setup and parser defects usually require a clean restart after the
wrapper is fixed; and transient host or license failures may permit a retry.
Retry eligibility depends on that cause. The run specification gives recovery
retries a declared maximum or budget, admission is rechecked, and a clean
restart or checkpoint resume uses only compatible, identified state. If an
upgrade caused the failure, reverting to the last pinned version creates a new
attempt rather than rewriting the existing record.

Safe caching follows the same identity and permission rule. A complete return
is reusable only when its project scope, permissions, inputs, transformations,
tools, libraries, PDK views, flags, conditions, and relevant state all match
the cache key. A technically matching checkpoint or cache entry does not cross
into another project, confidentiality scope, or license scope without explicit
authorization. Where a generator sits in the tool path, its context window is
part of that state, and it must be cleared between an open-source baseline and
proprietary work for the same reason a cache entry is not reused across scopes.
Partial and failed outputs may support diagnosis, but they are not served as
completed observations. Unknown dependencies invalidate the entry.

The 1996 Ariane 5 inquiry documented what happens when a reused component
carries an operating assumption into a changed system [@LionsAriane1996].

::: {.callout-war-story title="Ariane 5 and the reused alignment module"}
**The claim.** Flight-proven inertial-reference software from Ariane 4 was
reused for Ariane 5.

**The gap.** A 64-bit floating-point horizontal-bias value related to sensed
horizontal velocity was converted to a 16-bit signed integer under a range
assumption that held for Ariane 4.
Ariane 5 exceeded that range. The conversion raised an unhandled exception,
and the duplicated inertial systems shut down.

**The lesson.** A previously successful component can fail when its operating
conditions change. An architecture harness must record the version, range,
configuration, and surrounding state assumed by a wrapper or checkpoint, then
recheck those assumptions for the current request.
:::

The lesson is narrower than the accident. Reuse is safe only when the
conditions that made the prior execution meaningful still hold.

Tool isolation protects both the study and shared infrastructure. Each attempt
needs its own filesystem view, process boundary, resource limits, and timeout.
A malformed RTL candidate can otherwise corrupt a shared worktree, fill a
disk, exhaust host memory, or wedge a license process. The harness traps the
failure, retains partial artifacts, and returns control without treating the
candidate as measured.

Recovery and reuse choices remain in the affected attempt record. The enclosing
execution record joins the run specification and request to every attempt,
artifact, return, and cost, including failed work.

## Returned Records and Reproducibility {#sec-operational-attempt-record}

The returned record makes the runtime object model concrete. Across its attempt
records, the execution record preserves what was requested, attempted,
returned, and spent. Raw logs, reports, traces, databases, and counterexamples
retain details that a current parser may miss. Structured fields make status,
metrics, warnings, cost, and identity inspectable without rereading every file.
The execution record keeps both views because neither is sufficient alone.

This is a logical record, not a requirement to build a new database. A project
can map the fields and links onto existing run directories, scheduler records,
artifact stores, and review records, provided that attempt identity and
relationships remain recoverable. The enclosing record carries the study and
request context, preserves the ordered attempt identifiers, and aggregates cost
without hiding repeated or retried work.

At minimum, every attempt needs these fields:

- **Request and attempt identity:** Study, request, run specification, candidate,
  configuration, workload, software, conditions, and attempt identifier.
- **Starting state:** Exact inputs, source revision, artifact identities, and
  behavior-affecting state and versions needed to interpret or repeat the
  attempt.
- **Execution outcome:** Whether the request was refused or the attempt failed,
  was canceled, returned partially, or completed, together with terminal cause,
  termination confirmation, artifact and parser status, and retry eligibility.
- **Returned material:** Raw artifacts and logs, hashes, structured values with
  units, warnings, unclassified residual output, and artifact completeness.
- **Lineage and retry relation:** Parent inputs and artifacts, recorded
  transformations, whether the attempt is initial, a planned repeat, or a
  recovery retry, and any retry or reset parent.
- **Realized cost:** Amounts and units actually spent, including failed,
  canceled, repeated, and retried work.

Tool-specific extensions add meaning without changing the attempt identity. A
formal run adds its property, assumptions, bound, solver outcome, and proof or
counterexample. A physical-design run adds libraries, PDK views, modes,
corners, constraints, waivers, stage databases, and stage status. A sampled
simulation adds its seed, region, warm-up, checkpoint, thread count, and
declared sources of variation. Resource services may attach queue and run time,
compute, memory, storage, license occupancy, and reserved, consumed, or
billable amounts with their units and source. None of these extensions turns a
retry, stage, or resource report into a separate architecture result.

Unknowns remain explicit. An unavailable or unobservable value is marked
unreported or unknown, while a field that does not apply is marked separately.
A missing seed, library view, or raw report is not repaired by leaving its field
blank. Resource use is one part of the record, not a substitute for starting
state, status, lineage, or returned material.

What another architect can do with that record depends on who repeats the work
and with which setup. The Association for Computing Machinery (ACM)
distinguishes three related
claims [@ACM2020ArtifactReview]. *Repeatability* means that the same team uses
the same experimental setup to obtain the result. *Replicability* means that a
different team obtains the result with the same setup. *Reproducibility* means
that a different team obtains the result with a different setup. This chapter
uses *exact replay* as a narrower, book-specific term for submitting the same
retained request, artifacts,
versions, and recorded state again. A replay record shows that the same retained
inputs were requested; it does not guarantee identical realized execution or
output bits. For architecture work, all four claims still require agreement to
be interpreted against the property, variation, and operating conditions under
study.

The Popper Convention offers a systems precedent for putting experimental
steps, parameters, and dependencies in a version-controlled executable
workflow [@JimenezEtAl2017PopperConvention]. That practice can make an
architecture experiment easier to inspect and rerun, but it cannot by itself
package licensed tools, process design kits, or protected design data. Nor does
an executable workflow prove that two tool paths preserve the same architecture
meaning.

Hashes establish the identity and integrity of exact bytes. They do not prove
that two netlists are equivalent, two configurations express the same
architecture, or two runs support a valid comparison. Those relations require
the relevant transformation record and later check. The same distinction must
survive when one candidate branches through several tools.

## Multi-Tool and Multi-Fidelity Environments

Architecture studies often use several tools because no one tool observes
every relevant property. Multifidelity methods combine models whose cost and
accuracy differ for the quantity being studied
[@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. This chapter translates that
lesson to architecture tools. *Fidelity* describes how well a tool path
represents a named property under stated conditions, not one scalar ranking of
the tool. A path can offer high fidelity for one property and remain silent
about another. A simulation accelerated by a field-programmable gate array
(FPGA) may execute a target model much faster than RTL simulation without
providing application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) placement or timing
signoff. A circuit model may estimate SRAM area and access time without
executing the workload.

The useful comparison is what each tool actually models and what the
environment must retain to keep that result meaningful
(@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum).

| **Tool class** | **Representative use** | **What it models or checks** | **What the environment must preserve** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical or circuit model | Spreadsheet or CACTI-class SRAM estimate [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Encoded equations or circuit and technology assumptions, without workload execution. | Model version, organization, technology assumptions, units, and limits. |
| Compiler and software build | Target compiler, lowering passes, assembler, linker, libraries, and runtime image. | Whether the declared source and mapping produce the expected executable artifacts; no hardware timing or physical result. | Source and intermediate representations, target features, flags, mapping, library and compiler versions, diagnostics, and binary identity. |
| Functional instruction-set architecture (ISA) execution | ISA-level functional execution. | Instruction and software behavior under the implemented ISA model, without microarchitectural timing. | Binary, ISA options, input, termination state, and functional output. |
| Timing-model simulation | gem5-class processor and memory simulation [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5]. | Modeled pipeline, cache, interconnect, and memory timing under a configuration. | Workload, software, warm-up, region, seed, configuration, event counts, and traces. |
| RTL simulation | Verilator-class simulation [@Veripool2026Verilator]. | Cycle behavior under the supplied RTL and simulator semantics; no routed-delay result unless such timing is explicitly supplied. | RTL identity, testbench, compile flags, reset, waves, assertions, and logs. |
| Formal property or equivalence tool | Property checking or equivalence for a named model and relation. | The stated property or equivalence relation within declared assumptions, abstraction, and bound where applicable; no general correctness result. | Property and model identities, assumptions, abstraction, bound, solver version and outcome, proof or counterexample artifact, and cost. |
| FPGA-accelerated simulation | FireSim-class target simulation [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated execution of a mapped target model. The FPGA implementation is not ASIC signoff. | Target model, FPGA image, host configuration, workload, and returned traces. |
| Implementation flow | Synthesis, OpenROAD-class place and route, and stage-specific analysis checks [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. | Properties exposed by the declared stage, libraries, constraints, modes, and corners. | Every intermediate artifact, tool condition, warning, waiver, and stage result. |
| Fabricated silicon or lab hardware | Bench measurement of a device, board, or prototype. | Behavior and physical quantities exposed by the instrumented hardware under measured operating conditions; no coverage beyond the exercised workloads, conditions, and instruments. | Chip or board revision, instruments and calibration, firmware and software, workload, supplies, clocks, temperature, lab environment, procedure, units, and raw samples. |

: **Fidelity is relative to the property being examined.** The environment
retains each tool's model, inputs, conditions, stage, latency, and artifacts
instead of collapsing several returns into one generic score.
{#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[19,22,29,30]"}

Cost and property coverage determine which authorized branches a study can
afford to execute. The tool paths differ in resource regime as well as in what
they observe. Analytical models and compiler checks are often relatively cheap to
reconstruct from declared inputs. Cycle-level, RTL, and formal runs may be
long, resource-limited, or inconclusive. Implementation flows add persistent
databases, stage dependencies, and licensed features, while FPGA and silicon
paths add image or build steps, deployment queues, calibration, and scarce
hardware access. The environment records the realized conditions and cost
instead of inferring them from the tool class.

ZSim and FireSim illustrate one operational consequence. Throughput depends on
the realized configuration, not only the tool class. In one published
configuration, ZSim ran a detailed Westmere-class out-of-order model at 20
million simulated instructions per second, about $200\times$ slower than the
modeled core. The same study reported conventional detailed simulators at
about 200 thousand simulated instructions per second [@ZSim]. FireSim
reports a different regime. Individual target nodes in FPGA-accelerated
simulation can run at tens to hundreds of megahertz, while one 1,024-node
configuration ran at 3.4\ MHz for 3.2\ GHz targets, a slowdown of less than
$1{,}000\times$ [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. These rates are examples, not
constants. The modeled system, host or FPGA allocation, workload,
instrumentation, accuracy, and scale all change them. The environment therefore
records observed throughput and its conditions, and the method budgets from
that scoped rate.

SimPoint and SMARTS supply a separate lesson about sampling identity. SimPoint
selects representative program regions, while SMARTS supplies a statistical
basis for sampled simulation [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint;
@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The environment records the chosen regions,
weights, warm-up, fast-forward policy, and checkpoint parent. It does not decide
whether those choices support the intended comparison.

An architect can treat branch returns as observations of the same candidate
only when the recorded translations preserve the architecture meaning relevant
to each property. The execution record retains transformation, calibration,
and version identities together with branch-specific conditions so another
architect can check that correspondence.

For the prospective 3\ MiB candidate, the SRAM branch receives the exact cache
organization and declared process, voltage, and temperature conditions. The
compiler and runtime branch binds the baseline software image, target features,
libraries, flags, and runtime to an identified binary. The cycle-level branch
binds that binary and candidate to the XR workload trace, cycle-level simulator,
cache and power models, warm-up, seed, and checkpoint. RTL simulation adds the
generated RTL, testbench, compile flags, and reset. Formal checking adds one
named property or equivalence relation, assumptions, abstraction, bound, and
solver. Logic synthesis adds top-level constraints and libraries, while
physical implementation adds the floorplan, process design kit views, modes,
corners, and waivers. These branches are not interchangeable. Only the SRAM and
cycle-level branches participate in the hypothetical fixture later in this
chapter. The environment preserves every branch's input, raw and structured
return, cost, conditions, and limit without promoting or rejecting the 3\ MiB
candidate.

Chipyard makes this shared lineage visible. The cited framework documents paths
from one configuration through Chisel generation and Flexible Intermediate
Representation for RTL (FIRRTL) compiler passes to branch-specific tools for
RTL simulation, very-large-scale integration (VLSI) implementation, and
FPGA-accelerated simulation [@chipyard]. The simplified view here is not a
definitive map of every Chipyard component or version. The common configuration
supplies the shared lineage, while the branches produce different artifacts
and examine different properties (@fig-chipyard-framework).

![**A common configuration links distinct authorized tool paths.** This
simplified view of the cited Chipyard framework retains configuration lineage
while branch-specific transformations and tools produce artifacts for RTL
simulation, VLSI implementation, and FPGA-accelerated
simulation [@chipyard].](images/F6b-chipyard-framework){#fig-chipyard-framework fig-alt="A simplified flow diagram of the Chipyard paths described by the cited framework. A common configuration feeds Chisel generation and compiler transformations. Branch-specific tools then produce artifacts for RTL simulation, a VLSI implementation flow, and FPGA-accelerated simulation."}

The common configuration and generated hardware description provide a shared
parent, but branch-specific compiler and backend work determines the artifact
that each path consumes and returns. Shared configuration ancestry does not make
branch returns comparable. A comparison still requires matched artifacts,
conditions, and checks for the property at issue.

Shared lineage identifies related artifacts, but it does not determine when a
branch can run. ArchGym demonstrates that several architecture simulators can
share an interface under controlled budgets [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. A
project environment must additionally expose jobs that wait in queues, hold
licenses, resume checkpoints, and return at different times instead of hiding
them behind one `step()` call.

CHIA provides a current architecture-specific example of an open framework
that connects AI-directed hardware/software co-design work to heterogeneous
tool paths [@CuiEtAl2026CHIA]. Its integration is concrete, but the framework
alone cannot establish that every interface preserves design meaning, that
failures are safely contained, or that results will reproduce across other
projects and tool installations. The project environment must still carry
those responsibilities.

A dependency graph identifies which branches can run concurrently and which
must wait for an input. Workflow systems such as Nextflow and Snakemake show how
workflow logic can remain separate from execution on local machines or
computing clusters [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow;
@KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. Within the broader design workflow, the run
specification fixes authorized work, the harness coordinates it through a
scheduler adapter and backend, and Nextflow- or Snakemake-style workflow logic
expresses execution dependencies rather than owning design ordering, method
decisions, interpretation, or human review. The scheduler may plan authorized
work, but it may not add a tool, skip a required branch, or change fidelity
without a new request.

Applicable inexpensive prerequisite checks should run before expensive
dependent work. If a declared syntax, interface, functional, or equivalence
check reports that an artifact failed a predeclared prerequisite, the harness
records the return and suppresses only the dependent dispatch before synthesis
or physical implementation. This is not one universal tool order. The requested
run determines the prerequisites and affordable branches.

The prospective Lighthouse cache application brings these responsibilities
together in one run specification spanning pinned state, exact translation,
tool dependencies, failure handling, realized cost, and containment.

## A Prospective Lighthouse Cache Environment

This example applies the environment responsibilities to one narrow L2-capacity
study. It does not represent the complete XR tool graph.

The following scenario is hypothetical. Its thresholds and returned values are
author-selected illustrations, not empirical tool outputs or project history,
and they support no execution fact, validated measurement, comparison, or
architecture recommendation.

The setup first pins the candidate and fixed state, then defines the SRAM and
simulator request and return schemas. The run specification makes simulator
dispatch depend on the declared SRAM return, sets attempt and time budgets,
defines authorized resource and license use, and states the reset and retry
policy. The harness then retains every return and its realized cost.

Before any tool starts, the run specification collects those responsibilities
(@tbl-environment-contract). Its dispatch condition authorizes a cycle-level
attempt only after a complete, schema-valid SRAM return meets both thresholds.
The condition neither validates a measurement nor rejects a candidate.

| **Run field** | **Prospective Lighthouse cache-study run specification** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidates and fixed state** | Bind the run specification and study revision to the 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB candidates. Only the declared `l2.capacity` value may vary. Keep cache policy, NoC, memory system, compiler, runtime, baseline software image, and XR workload trace fixed. Each candidate retains the complete SRAM organization, model, and technology identity. |
| **Translation and identity** | Serialize the declared capacity and MiB unit exactly into the SRAM model under the declared process, voltage, and temperature conditions and into eligible cycle-level simulator requests with the declared cache and power models. Retain the behavior-affecting schema, wrapper, parser, tool, model, flags, host or container, seed, and reset-state identities. |
| **Order and dispatch** | Run one SRAM evaluation per capacity before dependent cycle-level work. Dispatch the cycle-level simulator only when the SRAM return is complete, its schema is valid, area is at most $1.5\,\mathrm{mm}^2$, and access time is at most $2.5\,\mathrm{ns}$. |
| **Matched work and limits** | Run the shared 2\ MiB baseline and every eligible alternative under matched conditions. Allow three SRAM evaluations and at most four cycle-level attempts, including recovery retries. Enforce queue-wait, run-time, and absolute deadlines, and stop when authorized work completes, no alternative qualifies, or a budget expires. |
| **Failures and recovery** | Keep invalid requests, timeouts, cancellations, infrastructure failures, stale state, missing output, and parser failures distinct. Link each recovery retry to its parent, charge it against the budget, and regenerate a clean working directory from the fixed state. |
| **Containment and reuse** | Grant only the declared tools, paths, credentials, network access, and resources. Quarantine output after unconfirmed termination. Reuse a complete return only when the request, candidate, conditions, translated inputs, tools, wrappers, parsers, and retained artifacts match. |
| **Returns, cost, and lineage** | Retain SRAM area, access time, energy and leakage; matched frame records, frame-time inputs, capacity misses, subsystem power, and warnings; translated inputs, commands, raw logs, parsed fields, residual output, hashes, resource use, cost, and parent-child lineage. |
| **Decisions left outside** | The environment does not decide whether a field is a valid measurement, two returns form a valid comparison, a reported limit establishes rejection, or a candidate should advance. |

: **This prospective specification illustrates runtime responsibilities; it is
not an executed study record.** The request, translation, state, expected
outputs, failure behavior, cost, and limits would be fixed before invocation.
{#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The chronology starts with three SRAM screens. The 2\ MiB rerun baseline and
the 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB alternatives would return areas of $1.2$, $1.4$, and
$1.7\,\mathrm{mm}^2$ and access times of $2.1$, $2.4$, and
$2.8\,\mathrm{ns}$, respectively. The first two candidates meet both declared
thresholds. The 4\ MiB candidate does not, so the run specification authorizes
no dependent cycle-level dispatch for it. The values alone would not establish
that decision without the parse status and recorded dispatch outcome.

The eligible candidates then enter matched cycle-level runs under the
four-attempt budget. The baseline would return subsystem dynamic plus leakage
power of $2.90\,\mathrm{W}$. The first 3\ MiB attempt would encounter a
stale-state setup failure, which authorizes a controlled retry from a clean
reset. A separate planned repeat follows. These attempts exhaust the budget.
The recovery retry and planned repeat would return frame, cache, and power
fields, but their values remain unreported. A summary derived from them would
be another artifact, not another tool call.

The resulting record would need to connect the three candidates, their
screening returns, the eligible cycle-level work, the failed attempt, the retry
and reset links, the planned repeat, every artifact, and total realized cost.
This example leaves the artifact identities, resource use, cost, output lineage,
exact translated inputs and hashes, behavior-affecting versions, starting and
reset-state identities, seeds and job times, parser and raw-artifact identities,
and matched frame records unreported. The record is therefore incomplete under
@tbl-environment-contract and the execution-record idea introduced in
@sec-architecture-20-ontology. @sec-feedback-verification-trust determines
whether any complete return can become a valid measurement, comparison, or
basis for advancing a candidate.

The harness keeps one exact identity connected across candidate state,
translation, execution, reuse, and return. Separate dispatch conditions,
budgets, deadlines, and stopping rules prevent an eligible candidate from
authorizing unlimited work. Recovery consumes budget and preserves its parent,
while containment and retention keep failed or uncertain work reviewable
without admitting it as a completed return.

This specification must still be written before the first tool call. Filled
afterward, it cannot refuse a bad translation or require a missing output. It
may authorize host selection, license reservation, pause, and resume, but
substituting a tool path, serving stale state, or skipping the baseline requires
a new request.

## Common Pitfalls

Building an environment that connects automated methods to architecture tools introduces subtle hazards. When a tool crashes or rejects an input, a naive integration might attempt a repair simply to let the tool run. However, fixing a runtime error without preserving architecture semantics invalidates the subsequent study. Projects frequently encounter two related failure modes:

**Repairing a request by silently changing the design.** A wrapper that repairs malformed inputs by injecting defaults, substituting units, or adjusting cache geometry to make a configuration legal may produce a clean tool exit. The hazard is that the tool evaluated a different candidate than the study requested. The resulting comparison is invalid, which compromises any downstream design decisions based on that execution.

**Treating a retry as a new candidate.** When a failed job is retried or a cached artifact is reused, the new attempt must carry its original parent identity, starting state, and cumulative cost. If a retry loses its lineage, an automated method may treat it as a distinct candidate. This double-counts the evaluation evidence, hides the realized cost of the tool path, and makes the sequence irreproducible.

## Open Questions

Automating architecture exploration demands more than just stringing tool commands together; it requires rigorous mechanical containment and semantic precision. The frontier established in this chapter lies precisely where execution discipline meets architecture intent, a boundary where hidden state, silent tool defaults, and incompatible representations routinely compromise otherwise sound experiments. Resolving these mechanics is far from a routine engineering chore. Ensuring that an automated method safely binds a candidate to its true performance, cost, and lineage across multi-fidelity environments is a fundamental research challenge. These translation and containment problems are deep enough to anchor a doctoral dissertation or a rigorous research paper, because until they are solved, the scale and velocity promised by AI-assisted design will merely generate irreproducible artifacts rather than actionable architecture evidence.

**Preserving architecture meaning across tools.** Tool wrappers and harnesses
must preserve the exact requested changes and safely expose differences in
returned values, without overstepping by interpreting the architecture decision.

- **How can an automated method verify that a tool translation preserves the
  requested architecture change?** We know that basic syntax and type checks
  miss critical errors like silent defaults, rounding, unexpected generated
  collateral, and unsupported tool combinations. The open research problem is
  how to rigorously compare the semantics of an incoming request against the
  translated artifact without rigidly rejecting harmless, tool-specific syntax
  repairs.

- **How can an AI-assisted environment expose semantic differences among tool
  returns that look operationally alike?** When combining multi-fidelity tools,
  matching identities and numeric fields can hide profound differences in
  modeled properties, assumptions, units, design stages, and fidelities. The
  environment must make these structural differences explicit to the study
  without unilaterally deciding what architecture claim they actually support.

**Keeping execution valid and contained.** Long-running architecture tools,
especially those used in physical design or cycle-level simulation, retain
complex state and require access to shared files, machines, licenses, and
intellectual property. The environment must survive failures and state changes
without confusing the work or silently enlarging its authority.

- **How can an AI-assisted environment determine that a stateful architecture
  tool has returned to a valid starting state?** Working directories, persistent
  databases, caches, checkpoints, random seeds, and host libraries often survive
  restarts. A robust reset mechanism must clear influential, run-specific state
  without incurring the overhead of completely recreating the tool session for
  every attempt.

- **How can an environment safely preserve useful partial or delayed tool
  results after the architecture state changes?** Intermediate data (like an
  early placement map or a partial simulation trace) may remain diagnostically
  useful even when it no longer describes the current candidate. Carelessly
  reusing it can mix incompatible states, while eagerly discarding it wastes
  expensive simulation or physical-design work. The open problem is tracking
  what remains semantically valid and carrying its lineage and conditions
  forward without accidentally admitting it as current evaluation evidence.

- **How can an environment grant an AI system only the exact access needed for
  one architecture tool action?** Generated scripts, RTL, constraints, and
  commands may require specific files, tool binaries, licenses, and host
  machines, but they rarely need broad system credentials or external network
  access. The challenge for system builders is designing strict, dynamically
  scoped authorization that grants enough authority for valid work while
  effectively containing malformed requests or adversarial actions.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Tool mechanics must not change the design being evaluated"}
**Principle:** A tool-connected environment must preserve the exact architecture intent across all translations, scheduling operations, retries, and parsing.

**Design Rule:** Wrappers are permitted to modify file syntax and command structure, and harnesses may manage execution state. However, they must never silently alter the requested architecture parameters or synthesize a completed return from a failed or partial run. You must retain separate, immutable records of execution status, raw artifacts, parsed fields, lineage, and realized cost.
:::

Preserving the requested design is not enough. The actions that reach the
tools also need a recoverable execution boundary.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Automate tool actions only inside a recoverable boundary"}
**Principle:** Tool automation must be completely contained within an isolated, strictly budgeted, and fully observable runtime boundary.

**Design Rule:** You must explicitly define finite budgets for elapsed time, compute, storage, and license usage per attempt. Cancellation operations must definitively confirm process termination and release of resources, quarantining any late-arriving artifacts. The environment must always be able to cleanly roll back an action or reset to a known-valid state; any action with irreversible effects or requiring elevated permissions must be subjected to an independent authorization gate.
:::

A tool transforms an artifact or analyzes a property, and a simulator is one
kind of tool. A wrapper validates, translates, invokes, and parses one tool. A
harness coordinates attempts, jobs, resources, failures, and records across
wrappers. The complete environment connects represented study state and
permitted actions to those tools and returns.

The prospective run specification states what may run, under which state,
authority, and budget. The execution record states what actually ran, returned,
and cost. Neither is a supported architecture claim. That claim still requires
the later checks that qualify a measurement, comparison, or decision. This
distinction also keeps invalid requests, execution failures, incomplete
artifacts, formal outcomes, and reported design-limit violations from being
collapsed into one result. Exact replay, repeatability, replicability, and
reproducibility remain separate claims, and hashes establish byte identity
rather than semantic equivalence.

Multi-tool and multi-fidelity execution extends the same discipline. Fidelity
remains relative to a property, and branches describe the same candidate only
when their translations preserve the relevant architecture meaning. The
environment can establish what was requested, executed, returned, and spent,
and it can preserve enough identity for replay and reproduction. It cannot
qualify a measurement, validate a comparison, or recommend a candidate.
@sec-feedback-verification-trust takes up that next task by determining how
returned values and artifacts can become useful feedback.
